posts.text: The example using the Text comma delimited is working. You must do something wrong. Or the light misaligned. Just put the Send VLL block and drag a Text variable in the vll code input and copy paste : 6,113,5,113,9,117,7,113 inside the text block. Then hit RUN. You cannot just put many scattered unconnected block around. The use of a text block is according to me, the BEST way to program a sequence of VLL code with ONE simple Send Vll code block: For the Third example, go in the "Lists" category, you will find there the "Create List with" block. By default, the "Create List with" block has 3 inputs, you can increase by using the blue gear option icon on the top left of the block. The for this block inputs, use the Math Number block which is the first block in the Math Category. Drag this little block in each inputs of the "Create List with" block. posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: Hi @Wert, Yes, my clock operates using a motor with precise angular position control. These LEGO motors feature an output shaft encoder that constantly tracks position within a closed-loop system. By applying the desired position increment every n seconds (a customisable setting), the motor only runs for fractions of a second at regular intervals. This results in absolute timekeeping precision (zero cumulative error) and zero maintenance—something that is virtually impossible to achieve with spring, weight, or pendulum driven clocks. One of the biggest engineering challenges was actually minimising friction and internal forces to protect the LEGO elements and the motor, as well as reducing system noise. The result is a smooth drive train, which I’m still fine-tuning for even better efficiency. Additionally, the system automatically handles daylight saving time shifts (summer/winter time transitions) and integrates custom LED lighting for an overnight display effect that I personally really enjoy. If you’d like to see the lighting setup, I’ve included a few photos on the LEGO Ideas project page (though keep in mind those feature earlier iterations of the build). The classic debate between Analog and Digital is timeless and universal—we see it everywhere, from music and photography to fine engineering. I personally love both worlds, as each carries its own unique advantages, philosophy, and charm. Thanks a lot for sharing your thoughts—if you have any more feedback or suggestions, they are always very welcome!

posts.title: [PC] Existence of Nivo card alternative to LEGO 9771
posts.text: Thanks for finding this. Gemini only found a network card: The Dutch NIVO project (Nieuwe Informatietechnologie in het Voortgezet Onderwijs, 1985–1988) was a national partnership between the Dutch Ministry of Education and three computer manufacturers: Philips, Tulip Computers, and IBM. Every participating secondary school received an identical standard package: three MS-DOS microcomputers, a shared printer, software bundles (including COMAL, MS-DOS, and word processing), and a proprietary local area network linking the machines. The dedicated hardware interface card powering that network was the Omninet network card. The NIVO Network Hardware: Corvus Omninet Because Ethernet cards in 1985 were prohibitively expensive for a rollout across ~2,250 schools, the NIVO project standardized on Omninet, a CSMA-based local networking standard engineered by Corvus Systems: The Interface Card: A standard 8-bit ISA bus add-in card installed into each school PC (the Philips P2000C / YES, Tulip PC Compact / Extend, and IBM PC XT 5160). On-Board Intelligence: Omninet cards were "smart" transceivers. Rather than forcing the host 8088/8086 CPU to handle packet framing and collision avoidance, the card carried an onboard Motorola MC6801 (or 6805) microcontroller and a custom gate array handling OSI Layers 1 and 2. Transceiver & Signaling: Omninet ran over balanced RS-422 differential signaling at 1 Mbit/s, using standard, unshielded twisted-pair (UTP) telephone-grade cabling daisy-chained across tap boxes. Network Topologies: Schools operated in small 3-machine clusters. One designated PC acted as the shared print/file server hosting the hard drive (typically 10 MB or 20 MB), while the other two functioned as diskless or floppy-based client workstations accessing shared network directories. Machine-Specific NIVO Interfaces While Tulip and IBM used conventional ISA expansion slots, Philips had to provide custom hardware bridges depending on the exact hardware delivered: Philips YES (Young Executive System): While mostly IBM-compatible in software, the physical bus architecture required Philips-specific expansion modules or daughterboards to accept the Omninet transceiver. Philips P2000C: For schools that received portable/all-in-one Z80/8088 hybrid P2000C units, networking required an external expansion slot module or a specialized slot-in Corvus interface tailored to Philips’s bus. The Software Layer: Constellation II & MS-Net The Omninet cards operated under Corvus Constellation II or OEM versions of Microsoft MS-Net: Shared Storage Volumes: The host PC's hard drive was partitioned into virtual volumes (Public, User, and System). COMAL & MS-DOS Deployment: Educational software—most notably COMAL-80 and MS-DOS utilities—was staged on the host PC, allowing students to boot or load language interpreters directly over the 1 Mbit/s RS-422 link without juggling 5.25" floppy disks. Evan again: So it didn't mention anything about Lego or I/O interfaces beyond networking. However, my next question was "Are there any experts on NIVO history?" and it gave me some good suggestions. I will email those people to ask for more information.

posts.title: [MOC] The Stinger Mantis- Physical Build
posts.text: At the start of the year, I finished a digital MOC of the Stinger Mantis from the Jedi series at lego's flagship scale and trying to largely keep their design schemes in mind. Since then I've been making slow bricklink orders to piece it together, and last week after some overtime I finally pulled the trigger on the remaining parts I needed (mainly some comparatively expensive slopes) The main goal I was trying to accomplish with this to incorporate the two separately rotating wings- using ratchet joints, the main wing rotates around the body, and the smaller wing with engine rotates separately with the ability to lock into place in the flight and landing orientations. Here it is in cruise mode- ignore the temporary stand, I haven't yet designed a UCS style stand for this model. (I honestly expected that my stud.io design would encounter errors somewhere and I'd have to spend a lot of time on fixing it, but it all works!) Here's a shot in landing position of the engines. You can see that it can sit in landing position without the stand- there's a slight tilt, so I may try to work landing gear for the outrigger engine into the V2. The mantis's unique cockpit shape is hard to accomplish with real bricks, but some panels make it so you can see out the front. Here's a shot showing how many figures you can fit in the interior- the only purist custom I have from fallen order is Cal, so I filled it out with pilots A better look at the interior- it was important to me to fit in the two-wide cockpit with comms station just behind. Past that we have the mission select table, living area with couch and table, and a very small representation of the kitchen. There's also a tiny version of the plant setup that's not very visible here but is signified by that yellow stripe on the back opposite the couch. For scaling, here it is alongside the 2019 Falcon. It's slightly longer but obviously also much thinner- I imagine it would retail for about what the falcon did. And it of course has an opening ramp on each side so Cal can go off on adventures.

posts.title: [MOD] Blacktron Battrax upgrades
posts.text: Since my Monorail upgrades won't be built in the near future, I decided to shift my focus to smaller vehicles first. First up is 6941 Battrax. The Battrax was an amazing vehicle that I couldn't appreciate as a kid (because I was as spaceship crazy as Benny). I love it now, but it still has plenty of things that always annoyed me. So it was time to give it some upgrades. Cockpit The cockpit always was a major point of annoyance to me, for 2 reasons. First, why extending the canopy if not using the extra space? Second, why are there so many openings? Front sides are wide open, preventing storage of anything in front of the driver. Even the floor has an opening right behind the driver. So I decided to rebuild the cockpit entirely. The original driver position has been moved 1 stud back, keeping its original controller tile for a navigator/operator co-pilot. In front of him sits the actual driver, with a steering wheel and his own control panel. All the holes are closed, so they can save their oxygen! Lastly, I got rid of the yellow base plate underneath that felt totally out of place when viewed from underneath. As a finishing touch, added an inverted curved slope to extend it smoothly to the nose. Wheels I never questioned the wheels at first. Until I set up a chase with the Space Police Spy-Trak I in pursuit. The Battrax wheels suddenly felt rather small. So I test fitted the Spy-Trak wheels on the Battrax (not the first person to do this), and that fits well after moving the rear axle 1 stud back. But those wheels didn't look right either. The Battrax looked faster, and those big wide balloon tires feel like a better fit on industrial vehicles that literally crawl forward. So I started looking at more modern tires and settled for a fairly new 55.9x22 model. This works for me! Flight unit controls Remember how the box and manual show the astronaut flying the top rear section without the cockpit attached? And yet, not a single button or lever is present at this seat! So I've replaced the longer slopes by shorter grille slopes, and added control levers for the pilot. Other stuff Replaced most of the printed grille bricks and tiles by moulded ones. Replaced the old hoses by thicker modern ones. This is yet to be tested in bricks when the parts arrive. If the new ones are too stiff and keep pulling the headlight bricks off I might revert back to the old hoses. At the bottom rear, I gave the base plate the same inverted curved slope finish as I did in the front.
